claims.text: The first patient was described as a 39-year-old right-handed woman; Table 1 separately gives age 38 when stroke occurred. She had migraines, obesity, dyslipidemia, no prior stroke, a 13-year history of smoking one pack daily, and negative family history of stroke or myocardial infarction. Sudden left weakness led to recognition of a right-hemisphere ischemic infarct. The body describes a parietal cortical site and the table a 1 cm posterior frontal focus; the precise site remains unresolved. Admission ECG was normal and BP elevated at 146/75, without a documented unit. Head/neck CTA showed no large-vessel occlusion or stenosis, and imaging showed no small-vessel ischemic disease. TEE showed an aneurysmal atrial septum, PFO with moderate right-to-left shunt even without Valsalva, and no thrombus. Left-MCA bubble TCD showed moderate-to-severe shunting. Heart monitoring showed no arrhythmia and named hypercoagulable tests were negative. Echo estimated LVEF at 50–55%, with normal RV systolic function, normal PAP 28 mmHG, normal LAP 11 mmHg, and normal RAP 3 with greater than 50% respiratory variation; the RAP unit is unstated.

After titration, CPAP at 12 cm H2O began four months after stroke. One month after initiation, use was 6 h/night on 100% of the last 30 nights, with residual AHI 0.6/h, adequate adherence and efficacy, and good tolerance. No stroke recurrence was reported two years later.

claims.text: A 46-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism, ongoing oral contraceptive pills, and current half-pack daily smoking presented with left hemiparesis and hemiparesthesia. Her father had a stroke at an early age. Admission BP was elevated at 169/58 without a documented unit. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with possible anterior infarct of undetermined age; myocardial infarction was not confirmed. Brain MRI showed acute-to-subacute right frontoparietal infarcts, and CTA showed no large-vessel occlusion. Bubble TCD was positive, Spencer Grade IV 101–300. TEE showed PFO, mild descending aortic plaque, and no thrombus or aneurysmal finding. Lower-limb venous Doppler was negative for DVT and named hypercoagulable tests were unrevealing. A loop recorder showed an ectopic beat without AF. Echo estimated LVEF at 45–50% and normal LAP at 6 mmHg; PAP was unreported and RAP not well visualized.

claims.text: A 59-year-old man developed sudden right weakness after briefly bending over in his garden, two days after a five-hour flight. He smoked one pack every other day since age 15; his father had multiple cerebrovascular accidents and his sister a hemorrhagic stroke. Outside-hospital admission vitals, EKG, and hypercoagulable workup were unknown; he later received acute stroke rehabilitation. MRA and carotid ultrasound were negative for large-vessel occlusion or stenosis. Historical TEE notes described probable small/tiny PFO, minimal right-to-left shunting, and no thrombus; the original report was unavailable. Echo estimated LVEF at 50–55%, with normal PAP 30.9 mmHg, intermediate RAP 10 mmHg, and normal LAP 8.4 mmHg. Plain TCD three months after stroke showed no focal stenosis but holocephalic diminished systolic upstroke, distinct from unavailable bubble-TCD data.

Admission BP was controlled and EKG showed normal sinus rhythm. MRI showed acute-to-subacute left superior cerebellar infarct without small- or large-vessel disease. Head/neck MRA showed an attenuated left vertebral artery without stenosis. Hypercoagulable workup was unknown. TEE showed small PFO, mild descending aortic plaques, and no thrombus or aneurysmal finding; Valsalva was unreported. Echo estimated LVEF at 55–60%, with normal PAP 32.2 mmHg, intermediate RAP 10 mmHg, and normal LAP 8.3 mmHg. Antiplatelet therapy was started and PFO closure was not performed.

claims.text: Repeat polysomnography two months after stroke showed mild overall OSA, AHI 14/h, severe supine AHI 80.5/h, and oxygen nadir 90%. A four-month CPAP titration was suboptimal without supine REM; auto-CPAP at 11–15 cm was recommended, without an inferred pressure-unit suffix. Machine receipt and a follow-up reporting 6.5 h/night use on 90% of the last 30 nights and residual AHI 1.9/h are both described at five months; timing remains ambiguous. A loop recorder was placed for high suspicion of AF and cardioembolism, with results unknown; neither was confirmed. No stroke recurrence was reported one year later. The figure caption additionally describes right-handedness and a 90-second PSG segment with qualitative oxygen desaturation, HR elevation, and EEG arousal; it does not supply exact trace values or whole-study duration.
